prompts.issue-planning:
Readers want to extend a loan by a week. Plan the work. This is the spec we agreed:

"A reader can extend their own loan by a week, once, unless someone has reserved the book. The lender is told about the extension. With no connection, the Extend button says it needs one. The Shelf API, in its own repository, needs a new endpoint for this."

The app talks to the API over plain HTTP, and both platforms allow unencrypted traffic
Signing in writes the reader's password to the device log
The session token is kept in unencrypted storage
A link in a QR code opens any web page in an in-app browser with JavaScript on

defects.title: The app asks to track location all the time, when it needs it only while searching
The reader's exact location goes to an analytics service and to the API, not just a rough area
Version 3.4.0 reads saved books from a new key and never moves the old ones across, so readers lose them
Adding a book changes the Redux state in place, so the list doesn't update
The book list draws every book at once in a ScrollView
The book list keeps polling after the screen closes, because the timer is never cleared
Loans load once and ignore a change of account, so the previous reader's loans stay on screen
The return button is an unlabelled icon with a small touch target
Profile text ignores the reader's text size setting
The loan card hard-codes colours instead of using the design tokens
Loading books never checks for a failed response and has no timeout

points.point: Lists the ways in, including signing in, scanning a QR code, finding books nearby, the librarian, and the calls the app makes to the API and to analytics.
Names what's worth protecting, including readers' accounts, their location and what they've borrowed.
Finds that a secret is built into the app, or that the app talks to the API over plain HTTP, and marks it missing.
Finds that signing in writes the password to the device log, or that the session token is kept in unencrypted storage.
Finds that a link in a QR code can open any web page inside the app.
Finds that the reader's exact location goes to analytics or to the librarian when it isn't needed.
Finds that catalogue descriptions from the partner reach the librarian's instructions, or that the librarian's reply can reserve a book without the reader confirming.
Treats the API as run in another repository, and marks the defences that live there as not checked rather than in place.
Marks at least one defence as in place where the app has one, and backs each defence it marks as in place with a file and line, not only a rule's name.
Considers a lost or shared phone.
Lists the missing defences as work to do, most serious first.
Keeps the rebuild rule: features move from src/legacy to src/features, and the legacy Redux store owns the book list while both halves exist.
Keeps that the Shelf API is a separate service in another repository, and describes only what the app uses of it.
Adds the parts the document is missing, such as the librarian, analytics, QR scanning and finding books nearby.
Notes that there are two ways to reach the API, the legacy client and the newer helper, and says which new code must use or treats it as a risk.
Keeps the rule that a change to how data is stored on the phone moves the existing data across.
Names each outside service the app sends data to, such as the Shelf API and analytics.
Marks what it worked out from the code as coming from the code.
States which parts or folders may depend on which, in a direction a reviewer could check.
Invents no parts, hosting or services the code doesn't show, and doesn't describe the API's insides as known.
Says a reader can extend only their own loans, and what the lender can see or do.
Covers a book someone else has reserved or asked for, and what the reader is told when they can't extend.
Gives acceptance criteria for each journey, including the ones that go wrong.
Covers what happens with no connection, since it's a phone app.
Asks, or proposes, how many times a loan can be extended.
Covers edge cases around the due date, such as a loan due today, an overdue loan, or the reader's time zone.
Says whether and how the lender is told about the extension.
Describes each screen or message in its loading, error and success states.
Covers use with a screen reader and large enough touch targets.
Leaves database tables, API endpoints and code to the system design.
Treats the API as another repository's: writes the contract change the app needs as a request to its owners, and doesn't design the API's insides.
Says what the app does when the request fails, hangs or there's no connection, with a timeout.
Builds the new screen in the newer TypeScript features, not the legacy half, reaching the API through one helper.
Handles pressing extend twice, so the loan is extended once.
Checks on the server that the loan belongs to the reader asking, as part of the request to the API's owners.
Names the tests that prove it, including a failed request and a double press.
Says how the loan's new due date reaches the screen, such as refreshing the loans the app holds.
Names the files that change in the app.
Writes it as a request to the API's owners in the other repository, not as a change it makes itself.
Designs the endpoint: what it takes, what it returns, and each error, such as the book being reserved.
Says only the reader who has the loan may extend it, checked on the server.
Makes a repeated request extend the loan only once.
Adds to the API without breaking the app versions already in use.
Uses the API's existing error shape and conventions, or asks what they are.
Returns the new due date in one date format.
Lists the questions for the API's owners, such as how many extensions are allowed.
Names src/theme/tokens.ts as the one place the tokens come from, and lists its colours, spacing and type sizes.
Finds colours written straight into screens instead of tokens, such as in the loan card or the librarian screen.
Finds the loan card's return button is an icon with no name and a small touch target.
Finds text that ignores the reader's text size setting, such as on the profile screen.
Gives contrast as ratios worked out from the token values.
Notes the older and newer halves of the app style screens differently, and says which new screens follow.
Sets touch target and text size rules suited to a phone.
Marks proposals as proposed rather than decided.
Makes the request to the Shelf API's owners its own item, and has the app's item depend on it.
Gives the items acceptance criteria from the spec: extending once, refusing when the book is reserved, telling the lender, and the message with no connection.
Plans the app's work in the newer TypeScript features rather than the legacy screens.
Plans nothing the spec doesn't ask for, such as a second extension or extensions of other lengths.
Names the spec, or where it came from, as each item's source.
Gives each item a goal and a first action.
